turns.content:
I take a Saturday morning ceramics class. Another regular named Julian always chats with me near the glaze tables, and every time he pulls out a fresh pack of spearmint gum, takes one, and offers me one. I usually accept out of reflex.

It's been three weeks now. I'm starting to wonder if he's hinting at coffee breath or if he just chews gum while talking.

I'm considering next time asking him, "Be honest, does my morning espresso breath carry across the room, or are you just generous with mints?"

Would that come across as insecure or awkward? Or is it fine to just keep quiet and take the gum?

Evidence you've reported: three occasions, he takes a piece himself first every time, then offers; he initiates the chats and keeps returning to the glaze tables with you. No reported comments, stepping back, or shortened conversations.

Conclusion: the pattern fits "he chews gum while talking and offers as a courtesy" better than "he's hinting." Someone dropping a hint about breath typically offers without taking one, or offers only sometimes, or reduces contact. Taking one himself every time and seeking you out are the opposite of both. Three data points is thin, but all three point the same way.

On your proposed line: it isn't insecure so much as low-yield. It's a yes/no question where "no" is the only socially available answer, so you'd learn nothing and would have made him manage your worry mid-conversation. If you want the information, get it from someone who will actually tell you (a partner, sibling, or close friend, asked plainly and after coffee). Self-checks are unreliable.

If you want to ask Julian something, keep it about him, not you: "Is the gum a fumes thing, or just a habit?" That gets you his reason without a loaded premise.

Practical baseline regardless of Julian: espresso does leave a measurable odor for roughly an hour, and water or a mint after it is a reasonable habit independent of anyone's opinion.

Recommendation: keep taking the gum, skip the question, and if the worry persists past a couple more sessions, ask a friend rather than him.

That's a solid read. I hadn't considered that him taking one first is actually evidence against the hinting theory.

- Your point about getting the info from a trusted source instead of Julian makes sense.
- I'm still mildly curious whether he offers gum to other people in the studio too.

I might casually watch for that next week before deciding anything.

Watching whether he offers others is a reasonable check, with limits on what each outcome shows.

- If he offers others too: supports the courtesy/habit reading. That would be the strongest evidence available from observation.
- If he offers only you: still ambiguous. He may only talk at length with you, or the pack may come out only during longer chats. It raises the hint hypothesis somewhat but doesn't establish it.
- If you can't tell (he's mostly at the glaze tables with you): no update.

Two things worth noting during the same session: whether he chews gum when you're not near him, and whether he takes one himself before offering to others. Those separate "chews while talking" from "offers to people."

One session is one more data point. If the observation is ambiguous, the friend-check route still gives a more direct answer than further watching.

I'll keep an eye on whether he offers to others. Hard to watch without being obvious while hands are in clay.

- If he offers to multiple people, I'll drop the question entirely.
- If it's just me, I might ask my wife about my breath after espresso. She'd tell me straight.

Does that plan sound reasonable, or am I overcomplicating a non-issue?

The plan is proportionate. Both steps are low-cost, reversible, and each outcome maps to a defined action, which is the opposite of overcomplicating.

One adjustment: the wife check doesn't depend on the observation result. It takes one question, gives you the actual answer, and settles the underlying worry whether or not Julian offers gum to anyone else. Doing it before Saturday means the studio observation becomes optional rather than load-bearing, and you can stop monitoring with clay on your hands.

If she says no problem: take the gum, drop the question, done. If she says yes: a mint after espresso fixes it, and Julian's motive becomes irrelevant.

Recommendation: ask your wife this week; observe Saturday only if you're still curious.

Good point. Asking her first removes the stake from the observation entirely.

I'll ask my wife tonight. If she says no issue, I can stop wondering about Julian entirely and just enjoy the class.

That's the right sequence. One detail for tonight: ask after you've had espresso, not at the end of the day, so she's evaluating the condition you're actually worried about. "Does my breath smell after coffee? Be blunt" is sufficient.

Whatever she says, the Saturday question to Julian stays off the table; her answer either closes the issue or points to a fix that doesn't involve him.

Asked her tonight. She said she'd tell me if my breath was bad, and it's fine after espresso.

So it was just Julian's habit all along. I'll take the gum, enjoy the class, and stop overthinking it.

Her answer is the relevant one: she has daily exposure and a stated willingness to be blunt, which is the best available check. It settles the worry that motivated the question.

One precision: it doesn't strictly prove Julian's motive; it shows there's nothing for him to be hinting at, which makes his motive irrelevant. Same practical result.

Plan stands: take the gum, drop the question, and no further observation needed on Saturday.
